video_title: Should Vitalik Leave the Ethereum Pitch to Others? - Uneasy Money
gist: Uneasy Money panel (host Kain Warwick, Austin Griffith, ex-core dev Greg of Sprinter) debates Vitalik's turn against the 'ultrasound money' burn meme and the lack of credible ETH-asset advocacy for Wall Street, core-dev vs app-dev tension over gas repricing, Ledger's post-signing telemetry and the case for passkey multisig wallets, and MegaETH's pivot to an on-chain AI inference marketplace exploiting the API-vs-subscription price arbitrage.

insights.claim: Vitalik Buterin pushed back on the 'ultrasound money' / ETH-burn narrative this week (around DevCon), which the host reads as a capitulation from memetic valuation toward arguing ETH is valuable for Ethereum's intrinsic properties.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Loss of the burn/supply-scarcity meme removes a simple ETH bull thesis; watch how ETH valuation narratives get reframed for institutions.
insights.quote: this feels like actually coming in a little bit harder and saying like this was a dumb meme

insights.claim: The ETH burn in EIP-1559 was, per the host's recollection, a late mechanism-design addition to a fee-predictability proposal, and it unintentionally spawned the 'ultrasound money' meme that came to dominate discourse with burn trackers and a focus on burning more ETH.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Narratives built on side-effects of protocol design are fragile; scarcity-based ETH theses depended on fee volume that has since collapsed.
insights.quote: it wasn't the intention the intention of 1559 to your point Austin right was not burn ETH. That was like a weird mechanism design choice

insights.claim: Austin Griffith argues EIP-1559's real benefit was wallet gas estimation and UX (transactions stopped failing), and that it effectively expanded block capacity; the burn was secondary.
insights.speaker: Austin Griffith (co-host, EF)
insights.so_what: Separates the durable UX value of 1559 from the speculative burn narrative.

insights.claim: If the goal is super-cheap transaction fees, generating 'revenue' from burned fees is incoherent; the burn mattered mainly because it was a good meme.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Fee-burn/'revenue' valuation models for ETH conflict with the scaling roadmap of cheap fees; don't anchor ETH value on burn.
insights.quote: why do we care about making money off the transaction fee?

insights.claim: Gas on Ethereum is now very cheap — roughly a penny to send a billion dollars — which undercuts any burn-driven scarcity argument.
insights.speaker: Austin Griffith (co-host, EF)
insights.so_what: Low fee burn means ETH supply is not deflationary via usage; valuation must rest on other properties.
insights.quote: it costs a penny to send a billion dollars

insights.claim: With ETFs and Wall Street now pricing ETH, the ecosystem needs far more careful, credible messaging than the meme-driven approach that worked when it was a smaller retail asset.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Narrative missteps now have larger price impact via institutional flows; watch for institutional-grade ETH research and messaging.
insights.quote: now that with we have the amount of ETFs the amount of you know everything else going I think we have to be like the the careful stairstepping we have is like significantly higher

insights.claim: There is almost nobody in or near Ethereum with deep credibility writing an investment thesis for ETH the asset aimed at Wall Street; mechanism-design researchers abound but asset-thesis writers do not (Brian Mosoff of Ether Capital was cited as a past example who is less active now).
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: A vacuum in credible ETH-asset advocacy is a structural headwind vs. Bitcoin/Solana narratives; the role is an opportunity.
insights.quote: name one person in anywhere in even in the vicinity of Ethereum who should be writing like research about the value of Ethereum like the asset

insights.claim: Ethereum's value is hard to compress into a short sound bite (decentralization matters only once you are censored), so the community repeatedly invents memes like 'ultrasound money' that end up failing.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Expect continued narrative churn for ETH; memes are a recurrent but unreliable price driver.
insights.quote: we keep trying to meme some easy way to make ETH valuable into existence and we keep failing

insights.claim: Panelists disagree on who should pitch Ethereum: Greg argues Vitalik is chief scientist and should be left to 'cook' while others (e.g., Etherealize) do marketing, as Bill Gates no longer pitches Microsoft; the host argues a founder must still hold a coherent thesis of why the thing matters.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev); Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Who owns ETH's institutional narrative (Vitalik vs. dedicated advocacy orgs) shapes how messaging lands with allocators.
insights.quote: like he is chief scientist not PR not marketing

insights.claim: A proposal to redirect block rewards Zcash-style to fund developers was floated around EDCON Sydney and met with EIP-999-style 'pitchforks', showing deep community resistance to protocol-level funding; burning is simply easier.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Protocol-level treasury/funding for Ethereum remains politically unlikely; burn persists by default.
insights.quote: it's more elegant just to burn it and not worry about it

themes.theme: Core devs vs. application layer and upgrade cadence

insights.claim: Ethereum's gas repricing work (e.g., SSTORE becoming more expensive) is drawing strong pushback from application developers, and core developers are reportedly going back to the drawing board on some changes.
insights.speaker: Austin Griffith (co-host, EF)
insights.so_what: Gas repricing can break deployed contracts (AMMs etc.); monitor hard-fork scope and app-dev objections as upgrade-delay risk.
insights.quote: application developers this is where this is my area pissed they they are really pushing back right now on uh the core developers

insights.claim: Core devs do care about apps, but the chain is a 'monolithic beast' where finding invariants is very hard — Greg says he once broke web3.js post-1559 and bricked apps due to an unknown invariant with MetaMask.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Protocol upgrades carry real breakage risk to app layer; expect hiccups on testnets and mainnet.
insights.quote: this thing's a beast. like an absolute like monolithic beast and yet changing stuff is like it's really hard to find the invariance

insights.claim: AI has sharply increased EIP submission volume — from roughly one a week to multiple notifications per day — overloading core devs who must also fend off long-dead proposals like EOF.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Governance bandwidth is a bottleneck; AI-generated proposal spam may slow or harden core-dev decision-making.
insights.quote: it was like one a week, you know? Like I subscribe to the Ebot the EIP bot tracker and I get a notification multiple times a day

insights.claim: Ethereum aims to accelerate to roughly three or four hard forks per year, helped by AI, but bundling ~30 EIPs into one fork means a single breaking EIP can delay everything.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Faster fork cadence would speed scaling features; watch whether fork scopes shrink to reduce all-or-nothing delays.
insights.quote: They want to increase the speed. They want to get like probably three, four hard forks out a year

insights.claim: Testing protocol changes against live state is extremely hard because protocols depend on many off-chain components and oracles; fork tests of Uniswap-like systems require configuring numerous oracle updates.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Upgrade risk to DeFi is underpriced; app teams should run AI-assisted fork tests ahead of hard forks.

insights.claim: The host's AGI benchmark: an AI that can compute his P&L on a given 2020 date for an address; his agent on ~900 transactions from that period still has 58 unknowns, with Fable 5.2 resolving issues like a Blur proxy contract changing its oracle pointer.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Historical on-chain accounting remains hard even for frontier models — relevant for tax/forensics tooling.
insights.quote: it's now down to it has 58 unknowns

insights.claim: Protocols loudly complaining that core devs broke them is partly marketing — public noise and dunking is 'good for business' and thought leadership, so upgrade debates will always look messier than they are.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev); Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Discount public outrage over hard-fork changes as partly incentive-driven signaling.
insights.quote: it's so good for business >> to make noise

insights.claim: The gas token built by the 1inch team caused major problems and drove gas repricing of storage; a related repricing bug that could cause an infinite loop in the VM went undisclosed for about two years (documented in 'Dodging a bullet' on the Ethereum security blog).
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Shows how app-layer exploitation of gas mechanics forces protocol changes and hidden security risks.
insights.quote: There's a blog post it's called dodging a bullet on the Ethereum security blog

themes.theme: Ledger telemetry and the hardware-wallet/clear-signing problem

insights.claim: Ledger's signing SDK sends transaction metadata to Ledger's servers via a POST request after a signing interaction — even on failed/errored transactions — allowing address-to-user correlation, which undermines Ledger's CTO's claim that server calls are needed for clear signing.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Privacy/security reputational hit for Ledger; tailwind for competitors and multisig/passkey wallets.
insights.quote: they do like a post API there's a post request so an API call to their server after a signing interaction happens containing metadata

insights.claim: Clear signing (ERC-7730) is roughly five years late; it standardizes how to read payloads, but implementation is left to wallets and Ledger says its devices lack memory to handle it, so it offloads to servers.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex); Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Signing UX remains a key attack surface; watch clear-signing adoption across wallets.
insights.quote: Clear signing is like five years late

insights.claim: The clear-signing standard relies on an on-chain registry anyone can add to but requires audits, and dynamic contracts (proxies, diamond contracts, ENS) cannot be hardcoded in firmware, forcing reliance on trusted signed servers.
insights.speaker: Austin Griffith (co-host, EF)
insights.so_what: Clear signing won't fully solve blind-signing for upgradeable DeFi; residual trust in servers remains.

insights.claim: Injecting third-party calls just before a transaction recreates the risk exploited in the Bybit hack via Safe (Gnosis), where code was inserted before signing.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Any pre-signing server dependency is a supply-chain attack vector; prefer wallets minimizing external calls.
insights.quote: Did did we not learn from by bit that like shoving [ __ ] just before a transaction is scary

insights.claim: Hardware wallets like Ledger are not suited for end users; they should be YubiKey-like signers plugged into a secure device, and power users effectively need a dedicated signing laptop (Grid Plus had the right idea).
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Expect security UX to shift from consumer hardware wallets to multisig/passkey setups; weakens Ledger's moat.
insights.quote: I think it just proves this like these devices are just not meant for end users

insights.claim: An iOS sandbox flaw (patched via hotfix) let another app steal a crypto wallet's signing, reinforcing the need for multisigs with limits and circuit breakers regardless of device.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Mobile wallet security relies on OS integrity; smart-account limits mitigate device-level failures.
insights.quote: Like the sandbox broke and they did a hot pack

insights.claim: Polymarket was hacked (around the time of a Binance-related hack) via a dependency on an analytics tracker in its website, illustrating supply-chain risk from injected third-party code.
insights.speaker: Panelist
insights.so_what: Front-end dependency risk is a recurring exploit vector for crypto apps; factor into app-level security diligence.
insights.quote: it got hacked because of a freaking dependency on an analytics tracker in their website

themes.theme: Wallet UX: apps, passkeys and multisigs

insights.claim: The optimal mobile custody design is a face-scan passkey (R1 curve signature) acting as a signer on a smart contract/multisig with spending limits, social recovery with a dead-man switch, and later optional hardware signers.
insights.speaker: Austin Griffith (co-host, EF)
insights.so_what: Smart-account/passkey wallet infra (embedded wallet providers) is the likely default custody stack for consumer crypto.
insights.quote: face scan it's basically a pass key you have a pass key that pass key is a signer on a contract that contract is a signer on a multisig

insights.claim: Users increasingly don't want wallets or browsing; they download single-purpose apps (Pump, Polymarket), so 'apps are so back' and security burden shifts to embedded-wallet teams, where future hacks will concentrate.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev); Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Value accrues to app-layer and embedded-wallet providers (Privy, Turnkey); their security failures are a key tail risk.
insights.quote: it's going to fall on all the like embedded wa

insights.claim: Regulatory fear under Gensler deterred DeFi teams such as Synthetix from shipping native mobile apps (Apple requires a company, creating a legal nexus), leaving DeFi UX stuck in dapp browsers; Infinex found integrating Synthetix unsolvable without rebuilding the interface.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Friendlier regulation unlocks native DeFi apps — a UX catalyst for DeFi adoption.
insights.quote: DeFi teams were scared to build a native app because it would mean they like had control of a thing

insights.claim: Cross-chain needs (especially Solana/SVM, where Safe-style multisigs don't port; Squads exists) mean the least secure chain dictates UX, pushing apps toward custodial 'database dollars' instead of self-sovereign money.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Multichain users favor custodial/database balances, a headwind for self-custody infrastructure.
insights.quote: the least secure place is the thing that dictates the UX

insights.claim: The UX bar is low — Canadian banks still use phone 2FA — so users will tolerate social recovery and similar steps; the industry overestimates the difficulty of onboarding.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Self-custody UX friction may be less of an adoption barrier than assumed.
insights.quote: the UX the bar is so low

themes.theme: MegaETH pivot and on-chain AI inference arbitrage

insights.claim: MegaETH is pivoting to become 'Mega' and build a blockchain-based marketplace for AI inference, per the host's conversation with its team.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Signals L2s repurposing tech toward AI; watch MegaETH token holder reaction and execution.
insights.quote: TLDDR mega ETH is turning into mega and they're going to be selling inference or creating a marketplace for

insights.claim: A large arbitrage exists between AI lab API rack rates and heavily subsidized subscription plans; a permissionless on-chain marketplace lets resellers distribute cheaper inference, and the host believes the delta must collapse.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Expect API/subscription pricing convergence and growth of inference marketplaces; watch for labs closing the arb.
insights.quote: you cannot have a an extremely valuable asset that you're selling with price discrimination like this and not have the world show up

insights.claim: Pivots from crypto to AI have been strongly positive EV — even teams that stumbled into AI pivots are doing better than the average crypto project — but public token holders react angrily to pivots that happen quietly for VC-backed private companies.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: AI pivots can rerate crypto projects, but expect holder volatility and backlash around announcements.
insights.quote: it's so positive EV if you're in crypto to pivot

insights.claim: Venice already runs a cheap inference marketplace with TEE/confidential compute options; staking VVV yields DIEM which grants a daily allotment of free inference.
insights.speaker: Austin Griffith (co-host, EF)
insights.so_what: Venice/VVV is a live comp for tokenized inference access models.
insights.quote: I stake my VVV and I get DM and I basically get some like daily amount that I can just use

insights.claim: Inference tokens are so fungible that any free-inference offering attracts abuse: a DevOps startup giving 15-minute free trials had to ban all of Indonesia due to stolen-credit-card abuse.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Free AI tiers are exploitable; resale markets for inference will grow, pressuring lab pricing.
insights.quote: They banned all of Indonesia

insights.claim: OpenAI is tweaking API pricing and plan economics to try to close the API-vs-subscription arb because it is unsustainable while it remains a trillion-dollar market.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: Expect continued AI pricing changes (cheaper APIs, tighter plans).
insights.quote: OpenAI is trying to close the OB

insights.claim: Greg argues the subsidy is likely smaller in aggregate than feared because many subscribers underuse their plans (a Spotify-like barbell), and that AI-market arbitrage patterns mirror crypto's over the past five years and will close.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Lab economics may be healthier than the 'subsidy' narrative suggests; arbs likely transient.
insights.quote: I guarantee you the subsidy is probably not as like nasty as people think

insights.claim: On-chain inference marketplaces still depend on off-chain APIs — the blockchain cannot see the GPU — limiting provability, though they enable autonomous DAOs or programs paying for their own inference.
insights.speaker: Austin Griffith (co-host, EF); Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: Temper expectations of 'decentralized AI' trust guarantees; value is mainly payments and permissionless access.
insights.quote: The GPU, the blockchain can't see the GPU

themes.theme: Ethereum Foundation lawsuit and org culture

insights.claim: The host argues the EF 'seppuku' clause controversy is a red herring: anyone whose top priority is removing it from foundation documents is negative-EV to employ, and firing a disruptive employee who also has cancer is distinct from firing for cancer.
insights.speaker: Kain Warwick (host, Infinex)
insights.so_what: EF governance drama is noise for ETH price but signals ongoing internal turnover.
insights.quote: it's so obviously negative EV to have that person around if that's the thing that they latch on to

insights.claim: The push for a more 'serious' EF yielded three serious orgs spun out of it, but a lot of good talent left the Ethereum Foundation.
insights.speaker: Greg (Sprinter CEO, former Ethereum core dev)
insights.so_what: EF talent drain and fragmentation into new orgs matter for Ethereum's roadmap execution.
insights.quote: We got three really serious orgs out of it anyway and the good talent like a lot of the good talent left
